projects.title: The Notwork
projects.description: The platform behind North Carolina's first state-backed esports and STEM league, where high schoolers learn, play and compete.
projects.longDescription: The Notwork runs North Carolina's first state-backed esports and STEM league. High schoolers use it to learn, play games, earn micro-credentials and compete. Teachers verify their students on it, and the league's staff run the whole season from it.
projects.role: Co-architect · led the build team · sole maintainer since Oct 2025
highlights: I was one of two architects. For the first build I hired and led five developers, set the coding standards, reviewed pull requests every week and worked through tickets with product and design.
In 2025 I led a rebuild on a new architecture: a redesigned schema, notifications end to end, server-side pagination, error handling and logging, and hundreds of regression tests.

Students compete in person, so they have to be who they say they are. I made teachers the verifiers, added roster and eligibility rules, and locked teams at playoff cutoffs. That replaced checking spreadsheets by hand.
AI helps judge submissions. It scores each rubric criterion, explains its reasoning and drafts feedback, and staff review and adjust every score before it counts.
I built mastery pathways with submissions, rubrics and micro-credentials, and an Explore feed that mixes lessons, video, games and student work.
projects.problem: The league ran on spreadsheets and separate tools. It needed one place where students could learn and compete, and where teachers and staff could verify students, manage rosters, send messages and publish content.
projects.solution: One Next.js app with a view for each role. Students get learning pathways, games and competitions. Teachers verify their students. Staff get the content library, rosters, messaging and analytics in one place.
projects.impact: It replaced the spreadsheets the league used to run on, and newer work runs on it too: AI-assisted judging, the lesson pipeline and the skilled-trades games.
features: Student profiles, teams, rosters, and leaderboards
Mastery pathways, submissions, rubrics, and micro-credentials
AI-assisted rubric grading
Game-based learning catalog (STEM, skilled trades, and more)
Curriculum, content, and post management
Teacher verification and student communication workflows
Notifications, email, and SMS via integrated providers
Season logic: roster locking, playoff cutoffs, in-season state
Staff tools: a 750+ item content library, rubrics, AI-assisted judging, SMS campaigns through Twilio, workflows, scripts, a test harness, and metrics

projects.title: AI Curriculum Pipeline
projects.description: Turns a rough lesson idea into a published lesson in nine steps. AI drafts each step, and a person approves it before the next one runs.
projects.longDescription: A pipeline inside The Notwork that turns a rough lesson idea into a published lesson. It follows the steps a curriculum team would: blueprint, outline, content, editing, fact check, media, formatting, audio and release. An educator picks the model for each step, from Anthropic, OpenAI or Google, and approves or redoes each step before the next one runs.
highlights: I modeled it on how curriculum teams build lessons, so each step has one job and a clear output.
Each step can run on a different model: Claude, GPT or Gemini, with Gemini making the lesson images.
A person stays in the loop. Each step gets the last step's output as context, and an educator can refine or regenerate it before it feeds the next.
The editing step scores tone and readability and suggests line edits as before-and-after diffs. The fact-check step rates each claim's confidence and flags what needs an expert's review.
Generated images wait for an educator to approve or regenerate them. Approved ones go to the Cloudflare CDN and into the lesson.
Every finished lesson comes with narration and practice questions.
projects.problem: A good lesson took about a week to write by hand, and quality depended on who wrote it. The platform needed a steady supply of lessons with text, images and audio.
projects.solution: Nine steps, each with one job, that take an educator from rough notes to a published lesson. Every step can be refined or regenerated, and the finished lesson publishes straight into The Notwork.
projects.impact: A lesson that took about a week now takes half an hour or less, and the lessons come out more consistent than the hand-written ones. More than 50 have been published so far.
features: Nine steps: blueprint → outline → content → editorialize → accuracy check → media → formatting → audio → release
Per-step model picker across Claude, GPT, and Gemini
Per-step refine and regenerate with persistent context
Editorial scoring with suggested line edits
Fact checks with confidence scores and needs-review flags
Image generation with approve or regenerate, then CDN upload
Text-to-speech audio narration
Generated practice questions
Direct publish into The Notwork as a content item

projects.title: Skilled-Trades Games
projects.description: Short, scored games on electrical, plumbing, site safety and more, from 2D puzzles to a 3D job site. You can play every one in your browser.
projects.longDescription: Ten browser games for a skilled-trades program on The Notwork. They cover building in the right order, electrical, plumbing and HVAC, site safety and knowing your tools, from 2D puzzles in Pixi.js to a 3D job site in Three.js. Each one is short and scored, with levels, so it works as practice or as league content.
highlights: I designed and built every game end to end, without any game-development background going in.
I used AI to help scope the games, generate assets and iterate quickly.
Every game has scoring, levels and progression, so it works as practice on its own or as league content.
features: Scoring, levels, and unlock progression in every game
2D puzzle and arcade games in Pixi.js
A 3D isometric job-site inspection in Three.js (Site Audit)
Diagnose-and-fix service calls with a customer story (Circuit Breaker, Flow State)
Practice modes alongside scored runs in several games
Phone-first layouts that also work on desktop

projects.title: Grand Theft Autonomous
projects.description: A block-coding simulator and live event console for a state robotics competition, where students' programs drive real cars through a miniature city.
projects.longDescription: The robotics finale of a programming curriculum, and the robotics event at VESL's state competition in May 2026. Students stack code blocks into a mission program, test it in the simulator, then send the same program to a real SunFounder Zeus car on a grid "Smart City". Each car has to collect coins, avoid the cops and get back to the vault.
highlights: A drag-and-drop block editor with if/else, repeat and sensor conditions. One deterministic interpreter runs every program, so the simulator and the car behave the same.
Programs go to the car over WebSocket, and a gamepad can drive it live for practice.
Judges score by coin value (+10, +25 or +50) and take off 5 for hitting a cop. Every heat can be replayed, with a live strip of the car's sensors.
Spec tests keep the scoring and the map's fairness rules honest.
projects.problem: Students had learned programming logic in drag-and-drop games. At the state event they had to program real cars, live, in front of judges.
projects.solution: One app for practice and for the event itself. The same block program runs in the simulator and on the car, and the judges score every run from the app.
projects.impact: It ran the training, the testing and the competition at the state robotics event.

projects.title: Stiegler EdTech Website
projects.description: Moved the company's two paid web platforms, a WordPress site and a Bubble app, onto one Next.js app without breaking a legacy URL or a form.
projects.longDescription: I led the move of Stiegler EdTech's two paid web platforms, a WordPress site and a Bubble site, into one Next.js app on Vercel. It went live in September 2026 with every old URL and every form still working.
projects.role: CTO · planned and led the migration
highlights: I measured both live sites with a headless crawl at desktop and phone widths, rebuilt every page to match, and checked each one with a Playwright parity test against a snapshot of the old site.
All 198 old URLs still work, with permanent redirects from the retired domain and a checker that verifies every one.
Every form posts to one server action, with its delivery services injected so tests run against stubs. All ten forms were checked end to end at cutover.
More than 1,700 past form submissions, from August 2023 to September 2026, moved into Postgres, and site search is built from the rendered pages.
I cut the hero video from 26 MB to 6.4 MB and added an image pipeline for share cards.
projects.problem: The company paid for two platforms, each with its own pages, forms and data: WordPress, with paid plugins and an email add-on, and a Bubble plan for The Mothership.
projects.solution: One Next.js app on Vercel that serves both sites, keeps every old URL working and stores every form submission in one Postgres table.
projects.impact: The WordPress hosting, its paid plugins and its email add-on are gone, and Bubble dropped to its free plan. The cutover was checked end to end: every page, every old URL and all ten forms.

projects.title: Safe Bet
projects.description: A compliance prototype for sports betting: it tells a sportsbook whether someone may bet, and teaches gambling literacy alongside.
projects.longDescription: States, institutions and employers all set rules about who may bet, and a sportsbook needs a clear answer before it takes a wager. Safe Bet turns those rules into one of three statuses: prohibited, conditional or clear. It also has the lessons, attestations and records that move someone into compliance. I built it in 2026 as a working prototype on typed demo data.
projects.role: Freelance engineer for a startup client
highlights: A rules engine where the most restrictive rule wins, across seven categories of people barred from betting.
A sportsbook gets a legal citation, not the reason a person is listed, so a check reveals as little as possible.
Six views (admin, operator, educator, high school student, learner and college athlete), switched from one "View as" control.
A course across five topics (recognition, reasoning, influence, vulnerability and protection), with a presenter mode for educators and certificates for learners.
20 spec files cover the rules engine and the barred categories.

projects.title: VESL Cyber Command
projects.description: A browser game that teaches the command line through a cybersecurity story, used again and again at competitions and events.
projects.longDescription: Students play trainee operators who work in the command line. The first mission, Operation First Contact, is a secure digital dead-drop. It runs a simulated shell in the browser, with a tutorial, an explain command for when students get stuck, adjustable typing speed and four color themes. I built it for an earlier curriculum build-out, and it kept getting used for competitions and events in a cybersecurity curriculum.
highlights: A simulated shell where students run real commands, like ls, to finish story missions.
An explain command that walks students through the mission reports when they're stuck.

projects.title: Build the Carolinas
projects.description: Marketing site for Build the Carolinas, the skilled-trades careers brand of ABC Carolinas and VESL.
projects.longDescription: Build the Carolinas is the brand ABC Carolinas and VESL use to bring students into construction careers. I built its marketing site.
highlights: Pages for each audience (students, parents and employers) and for trade pathways like the Electrician Pathway, credentials, careers and salaries, sponsorships and events.
A working contact form for program inquiries.
The skilled-trades games link to it: their results send players to its careers page.

projects.title: CTAC — Careers in Technology Cohort
projects.description: A coding program for adults changing careers. I wrote the curriculum and taught about 130 people, and more than 100 were hired into full-time roles.
projects.longDescription: CTAC trained adults to move into software jobs. I went through it as a student, then came back to run it: I wrote the curriculum, taught it every day as the only instructor for two years, and supervised a third. I also worked with the sponsoring employers so each cohort learned what their hiring teams needed.
projects.role: Co-founder & Director of Curriculum and Programming
highlights: More than 100 of the 130 or so career changers I taught were hired into full-time roles at Charlotte employers, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Lowe's, Ally, Coca-Cola Consolidated and Truist.
Those 130 were over half of the program's 200 or so graduates, across three years of cohorts.
I led a four-person curriculum team on a cohort build for an outside client.

projects.title: hector-mono
projects.description: My public monorepo: this site, a recipes app, a bookmarks app, and an AI tools catalog, on a shared component library with strict CI.
projects.longDescription: Where I build in public: this site, a recipes app with sign-in and a Postgres database, Stash for bookmarks, and a catalog of AI and web tools on the AI SDK, all sharing one component library.
highlights: The backend apps keep clean-architecture layers, and lint rules enforce them rather than convention.
One design system: shadcn/ui components, with a lint rule that fails CI on any color or style outside the system.
Every pull request runs lint, typecheck and tests for the packages it touches.
I build it with Claude. I write a short spec before I prompt, read every change like a teammate's pull request, and the decisions are mine.
